claim: Mycolactone causes changes in endothelial morphology, adhesion, migration, and permeability that are dependent on its action at the Sec61 translocon.
source: We show that mycolactone-induced changes in endothelial morphology, adhesion, migration, and permeability are dependent on its action at the Sec61 translocon.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript including use of alternative Sec61 inhibitors.

claim: Mycolactone causes profound effects on proteoglycans driven by rapid loss of type II transmembrane proteins of the Golgi.
source: Unbiased quantitative proteomics identified a profound effect on proteoglycans, driven by rapid loss of type II transmembrane proteins of the Golgi, including enzymes required for glycosaminoglycan (GAG) synthesis, combined with a reduction in the core proteins themselves.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by proteomic data presented in Figure 3 and Figure 4.

claim: Knockdown of galactosyltransferase II (B3GALT6) phenocopied the permeability and phenotypic changes induced by mycolactone.
source: Loss of the glycocalyx is likely to be of particular mechanistic importance, since knockdown of galactosyltransferase II (beta-1,3-galactotransferase 6; B3GALT6), the GAG linker-building enzyme, phenocopied the permeability and phenotypic changes induced by mycolactone.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Mycolactone depleted many secreted basement membrane components.
source: Additionally, mycolactone depleted many secreted basement membrane components and microvascular basement membranes were disrupted in vivo during M. ulcerans infection in the mouse model.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by proteomic data in Figure 7 and in vivo histological analysis.

claim: Microvascular basement membranes were disrupted in vivo during M. ulcerans infection in the mouse model.
source: Additionally, mycolactone depleted many secreted basement membrane components and microvascular basement membranes were disrupted in vivo during M. ulcerans infection in the mouse model.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by histological and electron microscopy data in Figure 7.

claim: Exogenous addition of laminin-511 reduced endothelial cell rounding, restored cell attachment and reversed the defective migration caused by mycolactone.
source: Remarkably, exogenous addition of laminin-511 reduced endothelial cell rounding, restored cell attachment and reversed the defective migration caused by mycolactone.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by experimental data in Figure 8.

claim: Buruli ulcer is a neglected tropical disease caused by subcutaneous infection with Mycobacterium ulcerans.
source: Buruli ulcer (BU) is a neglected tropical disease caused by subcutaneous infection with Mycobacterium ulcerans, characterised by development of large, painless plaques or open lesions, often associated with oedema.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Buruli ulcer disease.

claim: Buruli ulcer is characterized by development of large, painless plaques or open lesions, often associated with oedema.
source: Buruli ulcer (BU) is a neglected tropical disease caused by subcutaneous infection with Mycobacterium ulcerans, characterised by development of large, painless plaques or open lesions, often associated with oedema.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the clinical presentation of Buruli ulcer.

claim: Buruli ulcer is most common in West Africa but is also found in other tropical and subtropical regions including Australia.
source: The disease is most common in West Africa but is also found in other tropical and subtropical regions including Australia.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the geographic distribution of Buruli ulcer.

claim: The lesion can be sterilised by a minimum 2-month antimicrobial treatment course with rifampicin and clarithromycin.
source: Although the lesion can be sterilised by a minimum 2-month antimicrobial treatment course with rifampicin and clarithromycin, the wounds can take up to a year to heal and can lead to permanent disfigurement, especially when diagnosed late (Yotsu et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Yotsu et al., 2018.

claim: Buruli ulcer wounds can take up to a year to heal and can lead to permanent disfigurement, especially when diagnosed late.
source: Although the lesion can be sterilised by a minimum 2-month antimicrobial treatment course with rifampicin and clarithromycin, the wounds can take up to a year to heal and can lead to permanent disfigurement, especially when diagnosed late (Yotsu et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Yotsu et al., 2018.

claim: Mycolactone is the critical driver of Buruli ulcer pathogenesis.
source: The polyketide-derived toxin mycolactone, generated by M. ulcerans, is the critical driver of BU pathogenesis (George et al., 1999; Sarfo et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to George et al., 1999 and Sarfo et al., 2016.

claim: Mycolactone causes widespread coagulative necrosis and fibrin deposition in patient skin tissue.
source: Continuous production of this virulence factor causes widespread coagulative necrosis and fibrin deposition in patient skin tissue, as it diffuses through tissue away from the infecting bacteria.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mycolactone's effects in Buruli ulcer pathology.

claim: Mycolactone is responsible for the restricted immune response seen in Buruli ulcer.
source: Mycolactone is also responsible for the restricted immune response seen in BU.
evidence: This statement is supported by subsequent citations about mycolactone's effects on immune cells.

claim: Mycolactone shows long-term cytotoxicity to immune cells.
source: As well as showing long-term cytotoxicity to immune cells (George et al., 1999), mycolactone causes a rapid suppression of antigen presentation, co-stimulation and cytokine secretion at low doses (Guenin-Macé et al., 2011; Simmonds et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to George et al., 1999.

claim: Mycolactone causes rapid suppression of antigen presentation, co-stimulation and cytokine secretion at low doses.
source: As well as showing long-term cytotoxicity to immune cells (George et al., 1999), mycolactone causes a rapid suppression of antigen presentation, co-stimulation and cytokine secretion at low doses (Guenin-Macé et al., 2011; Simmonds et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Guenin-Macé et al., 2011 and Simmonds et al., 2009.

claim: Many clinical features of Buruli ulcer can be attributed to the inhibitory action of mycolactone on the Sec61 translocon.
source: Many clinical features of BU can be attributed to the inhibitory action of mycolactone on the Sec61 translocon (Baron et al., 2016; Hall et al., 2014), the complex that translocates most membrane, secretory and organellar polypeptides into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER; O'Keefe et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Baron et al., 2016 and Hall et al., 2014.

claim: The Sec61 translocon is the complex that translocates most membrane, secretory and organellar polypeptides into the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: Many clinical features of BU can be attributed to the inhibitory action of mycolactone on the Sec61 translocon (Baron et al., 2016; Hall et al., 2014), the complex that translocates most membrane, secretory and organellar polypeptides into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER; O'Keefe et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to O'Keefe et al., 2022.

claim: In co-translational translocation, nascent proteins are targeted to the ER surface by a signal peptide sequence at the N-terminus.
source: In co-translational translocation, nascent proteins are targeted to the ER surface by a signal peptide sequence at the N-terminus; the interaction between the signal peptide and the pore-forming protein of the translocon, Sec61α, opens a central channel that allows access to the ER lumen and a lateral gate through which transmembrane sequences can enter the membrane (Voorhees and Hegde, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Voorhees and Hegde, 2016.

claim: Mycolactone docks to Sec61, preventing signal peptide engagement and locking the translocon in an inactive state with the lateral gate open but the channel blocked.
source: Mycolactone docks to Sec61, preventing signal peptide engagement and locking the translocon in an inactive state with the lateral gate open but the channel blocked (Gérard et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Gérard et al., 2020.

claim: The biogenesis of most secretory proteins and Type I and II membrane proteins is inhibited by mycolactone.
source: The biogenesis of most secretory proteins and Type I and II membrane proteins is inhibited by mycolactone, while polytopic membrane proteins are largely unaffected (McKenna et al., 2017; Morel et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to McKenna et al., 2017 and Morel et al., 2018.

claim: Polytopic membrane proteins are largely unaffected by mycolactone.
source: The biogenesis of most secretory proteins and Type I and II membrane proteins is inhibited by mycolactone, while polytopic membrane proteins are largely unaffected (McKenna et al., 2017; Morel et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to McKenna et al., 2017 and Morel et al., 2018.

claim: Type III and tail-anchored proteins are resistant to mycolactone.
source: Type III and tail-anchored proteins, which utilise alternative translocation pathways (O'Keefe et al., 2021), are also resistant to mycolactone (Hall et al., 2014; McKenna et al., 2017; Grotzke et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hall et al., 2014, McKenna et al., 2017, and Grotzke et al., 2017.

claim: Proteins whose translocation into the ER is blocked by mycolactone are synthesized in the cytosol where they are degraded by the proteosome and selective autophagy.
source: The proteins whose translocation into the ER is blocked are synthesized in the cytosol where they are degraded by the proteosome (Hall et al., 2014) and selective autophagy (Hall et al., 2022; Gama et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hall et al., 2014, Hall et al., 2022, and Gama et al., 2014.

claim: Sec61 blockade by mycolactone induces an integrated stress response by activation of eIF2α kinases.
source: Sec61 blockade induces an integrated stress response by activation of eIF2α kinases (Morel et al., 2018; Ogbechi et al., 2018) and an increase in autophagic flux (Hall et al., 2022) and without resolution the cells eventually undergo apoptosis (Ogbechi et al., 2018; Bieri et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Morel et al., 2018 and Ogbechi et al., 2018.

claim: Sec61 blockade by mycolactone causes an increase in autophagic flux.
source: Sec61 blockade induces an integrated stress response by activation of eIF2α kinases (Morel et al., 2018; Ogbechi et al., 2018) and an increase in autophagic flux (Hall et al., 2022) and without resolution the cells eventually undergo apoptosis (Ogbechi et al., 2018; Bieri et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hall et al., 2022.

claim: Without resolution of Sec61 blockade, cells eventually undergo apoptosis.
source: Sec61 blockade induces an integrated stress response by activation of eIF2α kinases (Morel et al., 2018; Ogbechi et al., 2018) and an increase in autophagic flux (Hall et al., 2022) and without resolution the cells eventually undergo apoptosis (Ogbechi et al., 2018; Bieri et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ogbechi et al., 2018 and Bieri et al., 2017.

claim: For most human cells, the time from initial mycolactone exposure to cell death takes 3–5 days.
source: The time from initial exposure to cell death varies between cell types, but for most human cells takes 3–5 days.
evidence: This is a general statement based on previous observations in the literature.

claim: Endothelial cells are particularly sensitive to mycolactone.
source: We have previously shown that endothelial cells are particularly sensitive to mycolactone.
evidence: This statement refers to previous work by the authors.

claim: At low nanomolar concentrations, mycolactone depletes the anticoagulant receptor thrombomodulin.
source: At low nanomolar concentrations, mycolactone depletes the anticoagulant receptor thrombomodulin (Ogbechi et al., 2015) and junction proteins (Hsieh et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ogbechi et al., 2015.

claim: Mycolactone depletes junction proteins in endothelial cells.
source: At low nanomolar concentrations, mycolactone depletes the anticoagulant receptor thrombomodulin (Ogbechi et al., 2015) and junction proteins (Hsieh et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hsieh et al., 2022.

claim: Mycolactone increases the permeability of monolayers formed from endothelial cells derived from both vascular and lymphatic origin.
source: It also increases the permeability of monolayers formed from endothelial cells derived from both vascular and lymphatic origin (Hsieh et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hsieh et al., 2022.

claim: Thrombomodulin depletion has been observed in Buruli ulcer patient skin biopsies.
source: While thrombomodulin depletion has also been observed in BU patient skin biopsies (Ogbechi et al., 2015), this seems not to be the cause of the widespread fibrin deposition commonly seen within the skin tissue.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ogbechi et al., 2015.

claim: Thrombomodulin depletion is not the cause of widespread fibrin deposition in Buruli ulcer skin tissue.
source: While thrombomodulin depletion has also been observed in BU patient skin biopsies (Ogbechi et al., 2015), this seems not to be the cause of the widespread fibrin deposition commonly seen within the skin tissue.
evidence: This is an inference based on the authors' analysis of their data.

claim: Widespread fibrin deposition in Buruli ulcer is linked to aberrant staining for tissue factor.
source: Instead, this is linked to aberrant staining for the extrinsic clotting pathway initiator tissue factor (Hsieh et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hsieh et al., 2022.

claim: Tissue factor is normally located in the sub-endothelium where it is segregated from plasma proteins that drive coagulation and the surrounding dermal tissue.
source: Tissue factor is normally located in the sub-endothelium where it is segregated from both the plasma proteins that drive coagulation and the surrounding dermal tissue (Butenas et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Butenas et al., 2009.

claim: In Buruli ulcer patients, tissue factor was observed within the connective tissue distant from vessels.
source: However, in BU patients, tissue factor was observed within the connective tissue distant from vessels and this spatially associated with fibrin deposition and early signs of necrosis (Hsieh et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hsieh et al., 2022.

claim: Tissue factor in connective tissue spatially associates with fibrin deposition and early signs of necrosis in Buruli ulcer.
source: However, in BU patients, tissue factor was observed within the connective tissue distant from vessels and this spatially associated with fibrin deposition and early signs of necrosis (Hsieh et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hsieh et al., 2022.

claim: The integrity of the endothelium depends on adequate production and maintenance of the extracellular matrix.
source: The integrity of the endothelium greatly depends on adequate production and maintenance of the extracellular matrix (ECM) (Davis and Senger, 2005), junctional complexes (Wallez and Huber, 2008) and the glycocalyx, a highly charged coating of proteoglycans, glycolipids, glycoproteins and glycosaminoglycans (GAG) including heparan sulphate (HS), chondroitin sulphate (CS) and hyaluronic acid (Zeng et al., 2012) covering the luminal side of the endothelium (Reitsma et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Davis and Senger, 2005.

claim: The integrity of the endothelium depends on junctional complexes.
source: The integrity of the endothelium greatly depends on adequate production and maintenance of the extracellular matrix (ECM) (Davis and Senger, 2005), junctional complexes (Wallez and Huber, 2008) and the glycocalyx, a highly charged coating of proteoglycans, glycolipids, glycoproteins and glycosaminoglycans (GAG) including heparan sulphate (HS), chondroitin sulphate (CS) and hyaluronic acid (Zeng et al., 2012) covering the luminal side of the endothelium (Reitsma et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wallez and Huber, 2008.

claim: The glycocalyx is a highly charged coating of proteoglycans, glycolipids, glycoproteins and glycosaminoglycans covering the luminal side of the endothelium.
source: The integrity of the endothelium greatly depends on adequate production and maintenance of the extracellular matrix (ECM) (Davis and Senger, 2005), junctional complexes (Wallez and Huber, 2008) and the glycocalyx, a highly charged coating of proteoglycans, glycolipids, glycoproteins and glycosaminoglycans (GAG) including heparan sulphate (HS), chondroitin sulphate (CS) and hyaluronic acid (Zeng et al., 2012) covering the luminal side of the endothelium (Reitsma et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Zeng et al., 2012 and Reitsma et al., 2007.

claim: The enzymatic glycosylation of heparan and chondroitin sulphate is initiated in the Golgi apparatus by transferase enzymes.
source: The enzymatic glycosylation of heparan and chondroitin sulphate is initiated in the Golgi apparatus by transferase enzymes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GAG biosynthesis.

claim: The Golgi apparatus is the site of isomerisation and sulfation reactions needed to achieve the rich diversity of GAGs expressed at the cell surface.
source: This is also the site of the isomerisation and sulfation reactions needed to achieve the rich diversity of GAGs expressed at the cell surface (Yilmaz et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Yilmaz et al., 2019.

claim: The glycocalyx acts as an exclusion zone for blood cells and controls interactions with platelets, blood clotting factors and immune cells.
source: The glycocalyx acts as an exclusion zone for blood cells and controls interactions with platelets, blood clotting factors and immune cells as well as modulating fluid exchange and acting as a sensory system for the endothelial monolayer (Yilmaz et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Yilmaz et al., 2019.

claim: The glycocalyx modulates fluid exchange and acts as a sensory system for the endothelial monolayer.
source: The glycocalyx acts as an exclusion zone for blood cells and controls interactions with platelets, blood clotting factors and immune cells as well as modulating fluid exchange and acting as a sensory system for the endothelial monolayer (Yilmaz et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Yilmaz et al., 2019.

claim: The basement membrane is an ECM consisting of collagen type IV and laminins, crosslinked by perlecan and/or nidogens.
source: On the basal side of the endothelium, is the basement membrane (BM), an ECM consisting of collagen type IV and laminins, crosslinked by perlecan, a HS proteoglycan, and/or nidogens (Yousif et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Yousif et al., 2013.

claim: The basement membrane forms a scaffold that interacts with integrins on the cell surface, controlling structural stability, cell adhesion and angiogenesis.
source: This sheet-like network forms a scaffold that interacts with integrins on the cell surface, controlling structural stability, cell adhesion and angiogenesis as well as preventing leukocyte extravasation (Yousif et al., 2013; Song et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Yousif et al., 2013 and Song et al., 2017.

claim: The basement membrane prevents leukocyte extravasation.
source: This sheet-like network forms a scaffold that interacts with integrins on the cell surface, controlling structural stability, cell adhesion and angiogenesis as well as preventing leukocyte extravasation (Yousif et al., 2013; Song et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Yousif et al., 2013 and Song et al., 2017.

claim: Production of the glycocalyx and basement membrane relies heavily on Sec61-dependent proteins.
source: Production of these complex structures, which preserve and regulate the barrier between blood and tissue, relies heavily on Sec61-dependent proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known biology of these structures and the role of Sec61 in protein translocation.

claim: Mycolactone caused rapid changes in endothelial cell morphology and migration in primary human dermal microvascular endothelial cells.
source: Using primary human dermal microvascular endothelial cells (HDMEC), we found that, as well as increasing monolayer permeability, mycolactone caused rapid changes in endothelial cell morphology and migration, accompanied by loss of glycocalyx, adhesion and ECM proteins.
evidence: This statement summarizes findings presented in the Results section.

claim: Mycolactone caused loss of glycocalyx, adhesion and ECM proteins in primary human dermal microvascular endothelial cells.
source: Using primary human dermal microvascular endothelial cells (HDMEC), we found that, as well as increasing monolayer permeability, mycolactone caused rapid changes in endothelial cell morphology and migration, accompanied by loss of glycocalyx, adhesion and ECM proteins.
evidence: This statement summarizes findings presented in the Results section.

claim: Structurally unrelated Sec61 inhibitors, Ipomoeassin F and its derivatives, induced comparable phenotypes to mycolactone in a similar time frame.
source: Notably, structurally unrelated Sec61 inhibitors, Ipomoeassin F, and its derivatives induced comparable phenotypes in a similar time frame, highlighting the Sec61 dependency of ECM composition and function.
evidence: This statement summarizes findings presented in the Results section.

claim: The effects of mycolactone on cell adhesion and migration were dependent on ECM interactions and could be ameliorated by application of exogenous laminin-511.
source: On the other hand, the effects on cell adhesion and migration were dependent on ECM interactions and could be ameliorated by application of exogenous laminin-511.
evidence: This statement summarizes findings presented in the Results section.

claim: Mycolactone-exposed HDMEC cells began to take on an 'elongated' phenotype after 8 hr.
source: As in previous observations, the cells began to take on an 'elongated' phenotype after 8 hr.
evidence: This is based on time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1.

claim: After 24 hr mycolactone exposure, approximately half the HDMEC cells had an elongated phenotype.
source: The proportion of elongated cells increased with time (Figure 1A) and after 24 hr exposure, approximately half the cells (51.63 ± 2.89%) had this phenotype.
evidence: This is based on quantification of time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The average ratio of cell length to width doubled in HDMEC after 16 hr mycolactone exposure, and quadrupled after 24 hr exposure.
source: The average ratio of cell length to width doubled in 16 hr, and quadrupled after 24 hr exposure (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on quantification of cell morphology shown in Figure 1C.

claim: At 24 hr mycolactone exposure, a small proportion of HDMEC had acquired a rounded appearance.
source: At 24 hr, a small proportion (9.73 ± 4.01%) had acquired a rounded appearance (Figure 1B) similar to that reported for mycolactone exposure of fibroblasts (Gama et al., 2014) and epithelial cells (Guenin-Macé et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on quantification of time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1B, with comparison to cited literature.

claim: Mycolactone-exposed rounded HDMEC retained the ability to reattach to the culture vessel within 24 hr.
source: Notably, these cells retained the ability to reattach to the culture vessel (Figure 1—video 1), in line with their continued viability in this time window (Ogbechi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on time-lapse imaging data (Figure 1—video 1) and cited literature on cell viability.

claim: After 24 hr mycolactone exposure, HDMEC ability to re-adhere declined and the proportion of detached cells steadily increased.
source: However, after this time their ability to re-adhere declined and the proportion of detached cells steadily increased.
evidence: This is based on time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The elongated phenotype remained predominant in mycolactone-exposed HDMEC at 48 hr.
source: Although the number of rounded cells increased between 24 and 48 hr, the elongated phenotype remained predominant at this time point (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on quantification of time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Control HDMEC were able to close a scratch area within 24 hr.
source: While control cells were successfully able to close the scratch area within 24 hr, mycolactone-exposed cells displayed a gradual cessation in migration into the cell-free gap (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on scratch assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Mycolactone-exposed HDMEC displayed a gradual cessation in migration into a cell-free gap in scratch assays.
source: While control cells were successfully able to close the scratch area within 24 hr, mycolactone-exposed cells displayed a gradual cessation in migration into the cell-free gap (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on scratch assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: At 16 hr, similar numbers of control and mycolactone-exposed HDMEC had migrated into a scratch.
source: Thus, while at 16 hr similar numbers of cells had migrated into the scratch regardless of treatment, no further migration could be detected at 24 hr in the presence of mycolactone (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on scratch assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: No further migration could be detected at 24 hr in mycolactone-exposed HDMEC in scratch assays.
source: Thus, while at 16 hr similar numbers of cells had migrated into the scratch regardless of treatment, no further migration could be detected at 24 hr in the presence of mycolactone (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on scratch assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Mycolactone has been reported to cause cell cycle arrest.
source: However, it should be noted that mycolactone has previously been reported to cause cell cycle arrest (George et al., 1999), which can be a confounding factor in such migration assays and may explain this finding.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to George et al., 1999.

claim: Ipomoeassin F and ZIF-80 are structurally distinct to mycolactone but inhibit Sec61α in a very similar manner.
source: These are structurally distinct to mycolactone but inhibit Sec61α in a very similar manner since they compete for the same binding site (Zong et al., 2019; Pauwels et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Zong et al., 2019 and Pauwels et al., 2021.

claim: Ipomoeassin F and ZIF-80 phenocopied the 'elongated' appearance preceding detachment in HDMEC within 24 hr.
source: Importantly, both compounds phenocopied the 'elongated' appearance preceding detachment in HDMEC within 24 hr (Figure 1E & F).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: All three Sec61 inhibitors (mycolactone, Ipomoeassin F, and ZIF-80) showed similar effects on cell coverage and detachment in HDMEC.
source: As expected, cell coverage increased with time under control conditions, while the proportion of detached cells remained constant at approximately 5%. However, all three Sec61 inhibitors showed similar effects on both readouts (Figure 1G & H), with a similar effect of biologically purified mycolactone (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on time-lapse imaging analysis shown in Figure 1G and H.

claim: Cell coverage and detachment remained similar to control for approximately 24 hr after Sec61 inhibitor exposure, after which cell coverage declined with a corresponding increase in cell detachment.
source: Interestingly, both measures remained similar to the control for approximately 24 hr, after which cell coverage declined with a corresponding increase in cell detachment.
evidence: This is based on time-lapse imaging analysis shown in Figure 1G and H.

claim: Endothelial cell homeostasis is dependent on adequate Sec61 function.
source: Taken together, this data strongly supports that these changes are driven by Sec61 inhibition and that endothelial cell homeostasis is dependent on adequate Sec61 function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing similar effects of structurally distinct Sec61 inhibitors.

claim: HDMEC cultured under uniaxial shear stress maintained cell elongation and uniform alignment for 48 hr in the presence of DMSO.
source: Cell elongation and a uniform alignment of the endothelial cells was maintained for 48 hr in the presence of DMSO, as expected (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: HDMEC exposed to mycolactone under shear stress became increasingly disorganised over time.
source: By contrast, cells exposed to mycolactone became increasingly disorganised over time and by 48 hr a significant proportion were rounded and detached (42.6%, p<0.05) (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: By 48 hr under shear stress, 42.6% of mycolactone-exposed HDMEC were rounded and detached.
source: By contrast, cells exposed to mycolactone became increasingly disorganised over time and by 48 hr a significant proportion were rounded and detached (42.6%, p<0.05) (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is based on quantification of imaging data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Mycolactone did not cause a change in the proportion of elongated HDMEC under shear stress conditions.
source: Although mycolactone did not cause a change in the proportion of elongated cells under these conditions, the pattern of cell rounding was similar to that seen in static cultures (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is based on quantification of imaging data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: There was no detectable difference in the length:width ratio of HDMEC under shear stress at 24 hr mycolactone exposure.
source: There was no detectable difference in the length:width ratio at 24 hr, but by 48 hr mycolactone-exposed HDMEC that remained adhered were significantly elongated compared the DMSO control (p<0.001; Figure 1K).
evidence: This is based on quantification of cell morphology shown in Figure 1K.

claim: By 48 hr under shear stress, mycolactone-exposed HDMEC that remained adhered were significantly elongated compared to DMSO control.
source: There was no detectable difference in the length:width ratio at 24 hr, but by 48 hr mycolactone-exposed HDMEC that remained adhered were significantly elongated compared the DMSO control (p<0.001; Figure 1K).
evidence: This is based on quantification of cell morphology shown in Figure 1K.

claim: In uninfected mouse feet, fibrinogen was rarely detected, and then only within the vessel lumen.
source: Indeed, in uninfected (vehicle control) mouse feet, fibrinogen was rarely detected, and then only within the vessel lumen (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: At 21 days post M. ulcerans infection (Grade 1 lesions), fibrin(ogen) was seen within the blood vessel wall surrounding the endothelium.
source: In contrast, at 21 days post infection (Grade 1 lesions; metatarsal thickness increase ~10%), fibrin(ogen) was seen within the blood vessel wall surrounding the endothelium (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: After 28 days M. ulcerans infection (Grade 2/3 lesions), widespread fibrin(ogen) staining was seen outside blood vessels within the dermis.
source: After 28 days (Grade 2/3 lesions, metatarsal thickness increase 50–100%), widespread fibrin(ogen) staining was seen outside blood vessels within the dermis, in foci consistent with its conversion to insoluble fibrin (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Penetration of fibrinogen between the endothelial monolayer, through the vessel wall and conversion to fibrin within deeper tissue is consistent with previous findings in human Buruli ulcer patient punch biopsies.
source: This penetration of fibrinogen between the endothelial monolayer lining the vessel, then through the vessel wall and conversion to fibrin by other components of the coagulation cascade within deeper tissue is consistent with our previous findings in human BU patient punch biopsies (Hsieh et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hsieh et al., 2022.

claim: Extravascular deposition of fibrin is an early feature of M. ulcerans infection.
source: Furthermore, the changes in endothelial cell morphology and monolayer integrity described here and previously Hsieh et al., 2022 demonstrates that the extravascular deposition of fibrin is an early feature of infection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing fibrin deposition at early infection stages and cited literature.

claim: A total of 6649 proteins were detected in the membrane proteomics analysis of HDMEC.
source: A total of 6649 proteins were detected, of which 482 were significantly downregulated and 220 upregulated by mycolactone (>2 Fold change, p<0.05; Figure 3B, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on proteomic analysis data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 482 proteins were significantly downregulated by mycolactone in HDMEC membrane fractions.
source: A total of 6649 proteins were detected, of which 482 were significantly downregulated and 220 upregulated by mycolactone (>2 Fold change, p<0.05; Figure 3B, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on proteomic analysis data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 220 proteins were significantly upregulated by mycolactone in HDMEC membrane fractions.
source: A total of 6649 proteins were detected, of which 482 were significantly downregulated and 220 upregulated by mycolactone (>2 Fold change, p<0.05; Figure 3B, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on proteomic analysis data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 36.9% of total proteins detected in HDMEC membrane fractions were trafficked via the secretory/endolysosomal pathways that primarily depend on the Sec61 translocon.
source: Among the total proteins discovered, 36.9% were trafficked via the secretory/endolysosomal pathways that primarily depend on the Sec61 translocon (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on analysis of proteomic data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Sec61-dependent proteins represented 84.6% of the downregulated proteins but only 23.7% of the upregulated proteins in mycolactone-exposed HDMEC.
source: This group represented 84.6% of the downregulated but only 23.7% of the upregulated proteins.
evidence: This is based on analysis of proteomic data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Membrane proteins were the most affected in the downregulated group in mycolactone-exposed HDMEC, with little effect on cytoplasmic, cytoskeletal, mitochondrial or nuclear proteins.
source: As predicted, membrane proteins were the most affected in the downregulated group, with little effect on cytoplasmic, cytoskeletal, mitochondrial or nuclear proteins.
evidence: This is based on analysis of proteomic data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The downregulated fraction in mycolactone-exposed HDMEC included previously published endothelial targets of mycolactone.
source: The downregulated fraction included previously published endothelial targets of mycolactone including coagulation regulators thrombomodulin (TM), von Willebrand Factor (vWF), platelet endothelial cell adhesion molecule (CD31), endothelial protein C receptor and tissue factor pathway inhibitor (TFPI) and cell junction components tyrosine protein kinase receptor TIE1, angiopoietin-1 receptor (TEK), cadherin 5 (CDH5), junctional adhesion molecule 3 (JAM-3) and catenin β1 (Ogbechi et al., 2015; Hsieh et al., 2022; Figure 3—figure supplement 1), validating our dataset.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ogbechi et al., 2015 and Hsieh et al., 2022, and data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mycolactone preferentially targeted secreted and single pass type I and type II membrane proteins in endothelial cells.
source: As seen in previous proteomic studies and in vitro translocation assays (McKenna et al., 2017; Morel et al., 2018; Demangel and High, 2018; McKenna et al., 2016), mycolactone preferentially targeted secreted and single pass type I and type II membrane proteins in endothelial cells, with no effect on the EMC-dependent Type III proteins or the GET pathway-dependent tail-anchored proteins (Figure 3D).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies and data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Mycolactone had no effect on EMC-dependent Type III proteins or GET pathway-dependent tail-anchored proteins in endothelial cells.
source: As seen in previous proteomic studies and in vitro translocation assays (McKenna et al., 2017; Morel et al., 2018; Demangel and High, 2018; McKenna et al., 2016), mycolactone preferentially targeted secreted and single pass type I and type II membrane proteins in endothelial cells, with no effect on the EMC-dependent Type III proteins or the GET pathway-dependent tail-anchored proteins (Figure 3D).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies and data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: 51 out of 606 detected multi-pass membrane proteins were >twofold downregulated by mycolactone in HDMEC.
source: A small number (51 out of 606 detected) of multi-pass membrane proteins were also >twofold downregulated by mycolactone (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on proteomic data.

claim: The mycolactone-sensitive multi-pass membrane protein group was relatively enriched for signal peptide-bearing proteins (42% vs 4% amongst unchanged and upregulated multi-pass proteins).
source: This group was relatively enriched for signal peptide-bearing proteins (42% vs 4% amongst unchanged and upregulated multi-pass proteins; Figure 3E).
evidence: This is based on analysis of proteomic data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Higher signal peptide hydrophobicity and a shorter distance between the signal peptide and first transmembrane domain are associated with increased resistance to mycolactone in multi-pass proteins.
source: The rules governing sensitivity of this subgroup to mycolactone appear to be similar to those reported for single pass type I proteins (Morel et al., 2018), with higher signal peptide hydrophobicity and a shorter distance between the signal peptide and first transmembrane domain being associated with increased resistance to the effects of mycolactone (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Morel et al., 2018 and data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: 80% of the remaining mycolactone-sensitive multi-pass proteins contained at least one long loop (>50 aa) between transmembrane domains.
source: Of the remaining mycolactone-sensitive multi-pass proteins, 80% contained at least one long loop (>50 aa) between transmembrane domains.
evidence: This is based on analysis of proteomic data.

claim: 88% of the upregulated integral membrane proteins in mycolactone-exposed HDMEC were multi-pass membrane proteins.
source: Among the upregulated proteins, 88% of the integral membrane proteins were multi-pass membrane proteins, and only one of the predicted single pass proteins contained a signal peptide.
evidence: This is based on analysis of proteomic data.

claim: Only one of the predicted single pass upregulated proteins in mycolactone-exposed HDMEC contained a signal peptide.
source: Among the upregulated proteins, 88% of the integral membrane proteins were multi-pass membrane proteins, and only one of the predicted single pass proteins contained a signal peptide.
evidence: This is based on analysis of proteomic data.

claim: The four upregulated secreted proteins identified in mycolactone-exposed HDMEC are all secreted by non-conventional pathways.
source: Likewise, the four upregulated secreted proteins identified are all secreted by non-conventional pathways.
evidence: This is based on analysis of proteomic data.

claim: The majority of multimembrane spanning proteins utilise an alternative translocon that bypasses the lateral gate.
source: Overall, the data support the recently described model for the biogenesis of multi-pass proteins whereby the majority of multimembrane spanning proteins utilise an alternative translocon that includes Sec61 and the PAT, GEL and BOS complexes but, crucially, bypasses the lateral gate, instead relying on generation of a lipid-filled cavity on the opposite side of Sec61 (Smalinskaitė et al., 2022; Sundaram et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Smalinskaitė et al., 2022 and Sundaram et al., 2022.

claim: Only multi-pass proteins possessing a signal peptide or long internal loops require insertion into the membrane via the Sec61 channel, and therefore only these are sensitive to mycolactone.
source: Here, only those multi-pass proteins possessing a signal peptide or long internal loops require insertion into the membrane via the Sec61 channel, and therefore only these are sensitive to mycolactone.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proteomic data and the known mechanism of mycolactone action.

claim: The membrane targeted approach identified a higher number of Sec61-dependent proteins compared to previous studies.
source: Our membrane targeted approach identified a higher number of Sec61-dependent proteins in our control cells compared to previous studies (Baron et al., 2016; Morel et al., 2018; Grotzke et al., 2017) thus achieving our goal of wider capture of mycolactone-sensitive proteins.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the current proteomic data to cited previous studies.

claim: 100 of the downregulated proteins in mycolactone-exposed HDMEC were common to both the current dataset and siRNA-based Sec61α knockdown in Hela cells.
source: Moreover, when compared to siRNA-based Sec61α knockdown in Hela cells, despite the differences in cell type and methodology, 100 of the downregulated proteins were common to both datasets (Figure 3F; Nguyen et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Nguyen et al., 2018 and data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Possession of a signal peptide or anchor appears to be crucial to mycolactone sensitivity.
source: While possession of a signal peptide or anchor appears to be crucial to mycolactone sensitivity (Morel et al., 2018), overall, no specific signal peptide sequence features were associated with downregulation.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Morel et al., 2018.

claim: No specific signal peptide sequence features were associated with downregulation by mycolactone.
source: While possession of a signal peptide or anchor appears to be crucial to mycolactone sensitivity (Morel et al., 2018), overall, no specific signal peptide sequence features were associated with downregulation.
evidence: This is based on analysis of proteomic data.

claim: There was very little overlap between mycolactone downregulated proteins and those lost following knockdown of translocon-associated proteins TRAPβ or knockout of Sec62/Sec63.
source: In keeping with this, there was very little overlap between mycolactone downregulated proteins and those lost following knockdown of translocon-associated proteins TRAPβ or knockout of Sec62/Sec63 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3; Nguyen et al., 2018; Schorr et al., 2020), which assist gating of the translocon by weak signal peptides.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Nguyen et al., 2018 and Schorr et al., 2020, and data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Mycolactone acts via direct interaction with the Sec61α signal peptide binding site rather than through interference with accessory proteins.
source: Thus, as suggested by analysis of the structure of the inhibited translocon (Gérard et al., 2020), mycolactone acts via direct interaction with the Sec61α signal peptide binding site rather than through interference with accessory proteins.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Gérard et al., 2020 and is an inference based on the proteomic data.

claim: Gene ontology analysis of mycolactone-upregulated proteins supported previous observations of cellular stress responses.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis of mycolactone-upregulated proteins supported previous observations by ourselves and others of cellular stress responses, with significant enrichment of terms associated with oxidative stress and detoxification (Figure 3G; Morel et al., 2018; Ogbechi et al., 2018; Förster et al., 2020; Grönberg et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies and data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The upregulated proteins in mycolactone-exposed HDMEC included several proteins involved in the autophagy pathway, including SQSTM1/p62.
source: The upregulated proteins also included several proteins involved in the autophagy pathway, including SQSTM1/p62, which is involved in the cellular response to mycolactone (Hall et al., 2022; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hall et al., 2022 and data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the significantly downregulated fraction of mycolactone-exposed HDMEC, GO terms associated with glycosylation, matrix organisation, adhesion and cell migration showed the greatest over-representation compared to the whole genome.
source: However, in the significantly downregulated fraction a distinct pattern emerged, with GO terms associated with glycosylation, matrix organisation, adhesion and cell migration showing the greatest over-representation compared to the whole genome.
evidence: This is based on GO analysis of proteomic data.

claim: Within GO groups associated with glycosylation, matrix organisation, adhesion and cell migration, the vast majority of proteins detected in the proteome were downregulated by mycolactone.
source: Within these GO groups, the vast majority of proteins detected in our proteome were downregulated by mycolactone (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is based on GO analysis of proteomic data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The Golgi has a particularly high proportion of type II membrane proteins.
source: The Golgi has a particularly high proportion of type II membrane proteins as the membrane anchor and sequences around it can act as a signal for Golgi retention (Kikegawa et al., 2018) and nearly all of these Golgi-expressed type II membrane proteins were significantly downregulated by mycolactone (Figure 4A).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kikegawa et al., 2018 and data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Nearly all Golgi-expressed type II membrane proteins were significantly downregulated by mycolactone in HDMEC.
source: The Golgi has a particularly high proportion of type II membrane proteins as the membrane anchor and sequences around it can act as a signal for Golgi retention (Kikegawa et al., 2018) and nearly all of these Golgi-expressed type II membrane proteins were significantly downregulated by mycolactone (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on proteomic data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Type II Golgi proteins showed a higher degree of down-regulation by mycolactone than ER or plasma membrane localised type II proteins.
source: Interestingly, type II Golgi proteins showed a higher degree of down-regulation by mycolactone than ER or plasma membrane localised type II proteins (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on proteomic data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Mycolactone leads to significantly decreased abundance of multiple enzymes involved in both higher order N- and O-linked glycosylation.
source: Detailed analysis of our dataset revealed that targeting of Golgi-localised proteins by mycolactone leads to significantly decreased abundance of multiple enzymes involved in both higher order N- and O-linked glycosylation (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on proteomic data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The biggest impact of mycolactone on Golgi proteins is seen in GAG production.
source: However, the biggest impact is seen in GAG production, with the majority of the enzymes involved in GAG synthesis lost in mycolactone treated HDMECs (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on proteomic data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: All of the 23 proteins in the GAG biosynthetic pathway detected in the proteomic analysis are type II membrane proteins.
source: All of the 23 proteins in the GAG biosynthetic pathway detected in our analysis are type II membrane proteins and 19 (82%) of these were downregulated by mycolactone (Figure 4D), affecting every step of glycosaminoglycan production (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on proteomic data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: 19 out of 23 (82%) proteins in the GAG biosynthetic pathway were downregulated by mycolactone in HDMEC.
source: All of the 23 proteins in the GAG biosynthetic pathway detected in our analysis are type II membrane proteins and 19 (82%) of these were downregulated by mycolactone (Figure 4D), affecting every step of glycosaminoglycan production (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on proteomic data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Mycolactone affects every step of glycosaminoglycan production in HDMEC.
source: All of the 23 proteins in the GAG biosynthetic pathway detected in our analysis are type II membrane proteins and 19 (82%) of these were downregulated by mycolactone (Figure 4D), affecting every step of glycosaminoglycan production (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on proteomic data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Chondrointinase ABC treatment removed surface CS from HDMEC, resulting in fluorescence levels 60% lower than untreated cells.
source: As a control, chondrointinase ABC was used to remove surface CS, resulting in fluorescence levels 60% lower than untreated cells.
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data.

claim: CS fluorescence intensity was even lower in mycolactone-exposed HDMEC than in chondroitinase ABC-treated cells.
source: Remarkably, CS fluorescence intensity was even lower in cells exposed to mycolactone (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Mycolactone exposure disrupted surface HS expression in HDMEC (14.11 ± 7.40% vs. DMSO control 105.30 ± 9.79%, p=0.0006).
source: Similarly, using an antibody specific for a neoepitope of HS generated by heparinase III digestion, dHS, disrupted surface HS expression was observed in mycolactone-exposed cells (14.11 ± 7.40% vs. DMSO solvent control 105.30 ± 9.79%, p=0.0006, Figure 4F).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Heparinase III digestion revealed an abundance and diversity of heparan sulphate containing proteins present in untreated or DMSO-exposed HDMECs that decreased progressively with mycolactone exposure.
source: In addition, HS-containing proteoglycans were detected by immunoblot using the anti-dHS antibody. Heparinase III digestion revealed an abundance and diversity of heparan sulphate containing proteins present in untreated or DMSO-exposed HDMECs that decreased progressively with mycolactone exposure (Figure 4G, Figure 4—source data 2, Figure 4—source data 3).
evidence: This is based on immunoblot data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: By immunofluorescence, HS forms a mesh-like network around and between cells in untreated and DMSO control HDMEC.
source: By immunofluorescence, HS forms a mesh-like network around and between cells in untreated and DMSO solvent controls (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: In HDMECs exposed to mycolactone or ZIF-80, the HS-positive network was disrupted within 20 hr.
source: However, in HDMECs exposed to mycolactone, or ZIF-80, the HS-positive network was disrupted within 20 hr (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Endothelial B3GALT6 colocalised with the Golgi marker GOLGB1/Giantin in a perinuclear region in untreated cells.
source: Endothelial B3GALT6 colocalised with the Golgi marker GOLGB1/Giantin in a perinuclear region in untreated cells and was unchanged in those exposed to the solvent control (0.02% DMSO; Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: B3GALT6 expression levels remained normal in HDMECs exposed to mycolactone for 6 hr but a clear reduction was seen after 12 hr.
source: B3GALT6 expression levels remained normal in HDMECs exposed to mycolactone for 6 hr but a clear reduction was seen after 12 hr (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: ZIF-80 reduced B3GALT6 expression in HDMEC in a similar manner to mycolactone.
source: Notably, ZIF-80 reduced B3GALT6 expression in a similar manner (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: B3GALT6 siRNA-treated HUVECs demonstrated a similar elongated appearance to mycolactone-exposed cells.
source: B3GALT6 siRNA-treated cells demonstrated a similar elongated appearance (Figure 5C) and image analysis confirmed a significant increase in the ratio of cell length to width in HUVECs transfected with si-B3GALT6 RNA (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 5C and quantification in Figure 5D.

claim: Knockdown of B3GALT6 did not recapitulate the cell rounding phenotype induced by mycolactone.
source: However, knockdown of B3GALT6 did not recapitulate the cell rounding phenotype (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Exposure of mock-transfected HUVEC monolayers to 10 ng/mL mycolactone for 24 hr increased permeability to 23.13 ± 7.38%.
source: Exposure of mock-transfected HUVEC monolayers to 10 ng/mL mycolactone for 24 hr increased permeability to 23.13 ± 7.38%, an effect comparable to 100 ng/mL IL-1β (21.30 ± 3.48%; Figure 5E).
evidence: This is based on permeability assay data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: B3GALT6 knockdown in HUVECs led to a rise in monolayer permeability.
source: B3GALT6 knockdown in HUVECs also led to a rise in monolayer permeability (10.08 ± 4.37% and 15.47 ± 1.27% of the values seen in empty wells, p=0.2371 and 0.0367, for two different oligonucleotides, Figure 5F).
evidence: This is based on permeability assay data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: B3GALT6 knockdown did not reduce the rate of HUVEC migration in scratch assays.
source: Interestingly, B3GALT6 knockdown did not reduce the rate of HUVEC migration in scratch assays (Figure 5G); instead the cells exhibited a slightly increased healing rate compared to controls.
evidence: This is based on scratch assay data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Seven HS, CS, and/or DS-carrying proteoglycans were significantly down-regulated after 24 hr mycolactone exposure in HDMEC.
source: Our proteome revealed that seven HS, CS, and/or DS-carrying proteoglycans were significantly down-regulated after 24 hr mycolactone exposure (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on proteomic data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The most profound effects of mycolactone on cell surface proteoglycans were seen for perlecan and glypican-1 (detection at 10.8 ± 4.8% and 28.8 ± 9.0% of untreated control).
source: The most profound effects were seen for perlecan and glypican-1 (detection at 10.8 ± 4.8% and 28.8 ± 9.0% of untreated control, Figure 6B), while biglycan was partly reduced (43.7 ± 6.8% of untreated control).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Biglycan was partly reduced by mycolactone (43.7 ± 6.8% of untreated control).
source: The most profound effects were seen for perlecan and glypican-1 (detection at 10.8 ± 4.8% and 28.8 ± 9.0% of untreated control, Figure 6B), while biglycan was partly reduced (43.7 ± 6.8% of untreated control).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A ~50% reduction in perlecan was evident after only 2 hr mycolactone treatment in HUVECs, reaching significance at 6 hr.
source: A~50% reduction in perlecan was evident after only 2 hr mycolactone treatment, reaching significance at 6 hr.
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Depletion of glypican-1 by mycolactone was slower than perlecan, evident at 6 hr and reaching significance at 24 hr.
source: Depletion of glypican-1 was slower, evident at 6 hr and reaching significance at 24 hr (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Immunofluorescence staining of HDMECs showed abundant perlecan staining in control cells, particularly around intercellular junctions.
source: Immunofluorescence staining of HDMECs showed abundant perlecan staining in control cells, particularly around intercellular junctions, but the staining rapidly decreased in response to mycolactone, with reduced expression detectable after 8 hr (Figure 5C).

claim: Perlecan staining rapidly decreased in HDMECs in response to mycolactone, with reduced expression detectable after 8 hr.
source: Immunofluorescence staining of HDMECs showed abundant perlecan staining in control cells, particularly around intercellular junctions, but the staining rapidly decreased in response to mycolactone, with reduced expression detectable after 8 hr (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: HDMECs exposed to ZIF-80 for 8 hr displayed similarly limited perlecan-positive junctional staining as mycolactone-exposed cells.
source: HDMECs exposed to ZIF-80 for 8 hr displayed similarly limited perlecan-positive junctional staining (Figure 6C), and the depletion was duplicated when biological purified mycolactone was compared to synthetic material (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), and also occurred when the endothelial cells were under shear stress (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Numerous adhesion molecules and basement membrane components were downregulated by mycolactone, including nidogen 1 (NID1), laminins and collagens.
source: Numerous adhesion molecules and basement membrane components were downregulated by mycolactone, including nidogen 1 (NID1), laminins and collagens (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is based on proteomic data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The abundance of major basement membrane component collagen IV was not significantly influenced by mycolactone.
source: Although the abundance of major BM component collagen IV was not significantly influenced by mycolactone, perhaps indicating a slow turnover rate, several ER-localised and/or secreted enzymes involved in collagen biosynthesis, were reduced as previously reported in murine fibroblasts (Gama et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on proteomic data and cited literature.

claim: Several ER-localised and/or secreted enzymes involved in collagen biosynthesis were reduced by mycolactone.
source: Although the abundance of major BM component collagen IV was not significantly influenced by mycolactone, perhaps indicating a slow turnover rate, several ER-localised and/or secreted enzymes involved in collagen biosynthesis, were reduced as previously reported in murine fibroblasts (Gama et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Gama et al., 2014.

claim: Laminin α4 was seen in perinuclear regions within cells and in the network bridging intercellular junctions between endothelial cells in untreated and DMSO control HDMEC.
source: By immunofluorescence staining, laminin α4 was seen in perinuclear regions within cells and in the network bridging intercellular junctions between endothelial cells in untreated and DMSO control HDMEC (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: After 16 hr of exposure to mycolactone, the perinuclear laminin α4 staining was absent and the laminin-positive network between cells had become disconnected.
source: After 16 hr of exposure to mycolactone, the perinuclear staining was absent and the laminin-positive network between cells had become disconnected (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Loss of laminin α4 staining was observed in endothelial cells exposed to mycolactone under shear stress.
source: Loss of laminin α4 staining was also observed in endothelial cells exposed to mycolactone under shear stress (Fig Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The same striking decrease in laminin α4 was seen in HDMECs exposed to ZIF-80.
source: The same striking decrease was also seen in HDMECs exposed to ZIF-80 (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: After 24 hr mycolactone exposure, integrin β1, integrin β4, and laminin α5 in HDMEC were reduced to 45.0 ± 6.2%, 27.3 ± 7.7% and 15.6 ± 5.4% respectively of control levels.
source: After 24 hr, they were reduced to 45.0 ± 6.2%, 27.3 ± 7.7% and 15.6 ± 5.4% respectively of control levels (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Fibronectin levels decreased very rapidly in mycolactone-exposed HDMEC, showing >75% depletion after 4 hr exposure (p<0.01).
source: In addition, the loss of expression of the basement membrane component fibronectin and cell surface integrin α5 were validated using immunoblot analysis; fibronectin levels decreased very rapidly showing >75% depletion after 4 hr exposure to mycolactone (p<0.01; Figure 7—figure supplement 3, Figure 7—source data 2, Figure 7—source data 3) whilst the level of integrin α5 decreased more slowly, reaching ~50% of control levels at 24 hr (p<0.01; Figure 7—figure supplement 4, Figure 7—source data 4, Figure 7—source data 5).

claim: The level of integrin α5 decreased more slowly in mycolactone-exposed HDMEC, reaching ~50% of control levels at 24 hr (p<0.01).
source: In addition, the loss of expression of the basement membrane component fibronectin and cell surface integrin α5 were validated using immunoblot analysis; fibronectin levels decreased very rapidly showing >75% depletion after 4 hr exposure to mycolactone (p<0.01; Figure 7—figure supplement 3, Figure 7—source data 2, Figure 7—source data 3) whilst the level of integrin α5 decreased more slowly, reaching ~50% of control levels at 24 hr (p<0.01; Figure 7—figure supplement 4, Figure 7—source data 4, Figure 7—source data 5).
evidence: This is based on immunoblot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

claim: In mouse feet receiving the vehicle control, the dermis contained neutral glycans and the vasculature displayed an intact vessel basement membrane.
source: In mouse feet receiving the vehicle control (Figure 7D1), the dermis contained neutral glycans (purple staining) and the vasculature displayed an intact vessel basement membrane (Figure 7D4, insert).

claim: At early stages of M. ulcerans infection (Grade 1), immune cell infiltration could be seen in proximity to mycobacterial clusters and the surrounding dermal tissue had become more acidic.
source: At early stages of infection (Grade 1; Figure 7D2), immune cell infiltration could be seen in these regions in proximity to mycobacterial clusters (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and the surrounding dermal tissue had become more acidic (blue staining; Figure 7D5).

claim: At later stages of M. ulcerans infection (Grade 2/3), the dermis showed marked oedema and the fibrous architecture was disrupted.
source: At later stages of infection, when the metatarsal area was more swollen (Figure 7D3) and the dermis showed marked oedema and the fibrous architecture was disrupted (Figure 7D6–7), there was an overall reduction in the intensity of staining around the vasculature and the vessel basement membranes were irregular (Figure 7D6, insert).

claim: At later stages of M. ulcerans infection (Grade 2/3), there was an overall reduction in the intensity of staining around the vasculature and the vessel basement membranes were irregular.
source: At later stages of infection, when the metatarsal area was more swollen (Figure 7D3) and the dermis showed marked oedema and the fibrous architecture was disrupted (Figure 7D6–7), there was an overall reduction in the intensity of staining around the vasculature and the vessel basement membranes were irregular (Figure 7D6, insert).

claim: In Grade 1 M. ulcerans infection, the interstitium surrounding the capillary was expanded by electron-lucent granular material.

claim: In Grade 1 M. ulcerans infection, pericyte processes were often separated and collagen fibrils close to the blood vessels increasingly disaggregated.
source: In Grade 1, the interstitium surrounding the capillary was expanded by electron-lucent granular material, pericyte processes were often separated and collagen fibrils close to the blood vessels increasingly disaggregated.

claim: In Grade 1 M. ulcerans infection, the endothelial cells exhibited varying degrees of swelling and vacuolation with an irregular luminal surface including cytoplasmic undulation and projections.

claim: Primary HDMECs efficiently re-attached to laminin-511-coated culture vessels.

claim: Mycolactone-exposed HDMEC did not re-adhere efficiently to laminin-411 or laminin-111 coated vessels.
