source: On uncoated wells, mycolactone caused the expected phenotypic changes (Figure 8B–C), and remarkably, exogenous laminin α5 significantly reduced mycolactone-driven cell rounding, even after 48 hr (7.7 ± 1.5% vs 17.6 ± 2.4%, p=0.0153, Figure 8B).
evidence: This is based on time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Laminin-511 coating prevented the decrease in attached HDMEC seen between 36 and 48 hr in uncoated wells exposed to mycolactone (p=0.0123).
source: Similarly, while the relative number of attached cells did not increase steadily with time as for the DMSO control (Figure 8C), laminin-511 coating prevented the decrease in attached cells seen between 36 and 48 hr in uncoated wells (p=0.0123).
evidence: This is based on time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Laminin coating did not impact HDMEC survival in the presence or absence of mycolactone at 48 hr.
source: Laminin coating did not impact HDMEC survival in the presence or absence of mycolactone at 48 hr (Figure 8—figure supplement 3), although as mentioned before, cell death due to mycolactone is minimal prior to 72 hr (Ogbechi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on cell viability assay data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3 and cited literature.

claim: Control HUVECs took less than 16 hr to close a 600–800 µm gap in scratch assays.
source: Monitoring cell migration using time-lapse imaging revealed that control HUVECs took less than 16 hr to close a 600–800 µm gap (Figure 8—video 1).
evidence: This is based on time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 8—video 1.

claim: The leading edge of wounded HUVEC monolayers exposed to mycolactone gradually stopped migrating into the cell-free region after ~7 hr.
source: By contrast, the leading edge of wounded HUVEC monolayers exposed to mycolactone gradually stopped migrating into the cell-free region after ~7 hr; at this point the cells began to migrate randomly before undergoing the previously described morphological changes (Figure 8—video 2).
evidence: This is based on time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 8—video 2.

claim: In HUVEC monolayers plated onto laminin-511, cells continued to migrate into the gap in the presence of mycolactone, with a leading edge still evident after 16 hr.
source: However, strikingly, in HUVEC monolayers plated onto laminin-511, cells continued to migrate into the gap in the presence of mycolactone, with a leading edge still evident after 16 hr (Figure 8—video 3).
evidence: This is based on time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 8—video 3.

claim: HUVECs plated onto laminin-511 were able to migrate in the presence of mycolactone at a rate comparable to that seen in monolayers exposed to DMSO in uncoated wells (p=0.286).
source: Cell counts per unit scratch area at 8 and 16 hr showed that cells plated onto laminin-511 were able to migrate back at a rate comparable to that seen in monolayers exposed to DMSO in uncoated wells (Figure 8D, p=0.286).
evidence: This is based on quantification of time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Laminin-411 and laminin-111 did not show the same effects on migration as laminin-511 in mycolactone-exposed HUVECs.
source: We did not see these same effects on laminin-411 and –111-coated wells (Figure 8—video 4 and Figure 8—video 5) where migration rates remained significantly lower than the control (p=0.0054 and 0.0003, respectively, Figure 8—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 8—video 4 and Figure 8—video 5, and quantification in Figure 8—figure supplement 4.

claim: The ability of laminin α5 to reverse or diminish the impact of mycolactone on endothelial cell adhesion, morphology and migration highlights the contribution of the loss of basement membrane proteins to the phenotypic changes induced by mycolactone.
source: This ability of laminin α5 to reverse or diminish the impact of mycolactone on endothelial cell adhesion, morphology and migration highlights the contribution of the loss of basement membrane proteins to the phenotypic changes induced by mycolactone and presents an unanticipated potential for use in wound care in Buruli ulcer skin lesions, although such therapies are currently in their infancy (Iorio et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and cited literature.

claim: Laminin α5 presents an unanticipated potential for use in wound care in Buruli ulcer skin lesions.
source: This ability of laminin α5 to reverse or diminish the impact of mycolactone on endothelial cell adhesion, morphology and migration highlights the contribution of the loss of basement membrane proteins to the phenotypic changes induced by mycolactone and presents an unanticipated potential for use in wound care in Buruli ulcer skin lesions, although such therapies are currently in their infancy (Iorio et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the experimental findings and cited literature.

claim: The current work provides further evidence supporting a third and vital pathway to tissue necrosis in Buruli ulcer: the induction of endothelial dysfunction that drives an indirect mechanism leading to tissue necrosis via the breakdown of vessel integrity and fibrin-driven ischemia within tissue.
source: Our findings provide further evidence supporting a third and vital pathway to tissue necrosis; the induction of endothelial dysfunction that drives an indirect mechanism leading to tissue necrosis via the breakdown of vessel integrity and fibrin-driven ischemia within tissue.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the authors' interpretation of their findings.

claim: The current work reaffirms the critical role that Sec61 inhibition plays in the virulence mechanism of mycolactone.
source: The current work reaffirms the critical role that Sec61 inhibition plays in the virulence mechanism of mycolactone.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the authors' interpretation of their findings.

claim: The endothelium is particularly sensitive to functional perturbation of the Sec61 translocon.
source: This suggests that the endothelium is particularly sensitive to functional perturbation of the Sec61 translocon and perhaps explains why these cells are so exquisitely sensitive to the compound.
evidence: This is an inference based on the authors' unsuccessful attempts to express SEC61A1 mutants in primary endothelial cells.

claim: The primary target of mycolactone in endothelial cells is Sec61.
source: Hence, we are confident that the primary target of mycolactone in endothelial cells is Sec61, as it has already been shown in immune cells (Baron et al., 2016; Hall et al., 2014; Grotzke et al., 2017), fibroblasts (Hall et al., 2022) and epithelial cells (Ogbechi et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies and the current data showing similar effects of structurally distinct Sec61 inhibitors.

claim: Epithelial cells showed similar effects on migration to those reported in the current work on endothelial cells.
source: Since epithelial cells showed similar effects on migration to those we report here, these effects probably depend on its action on the Sec61 translocon rather than other previously proposed mechanisms such as WASP activation (Guenin-Macé et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Guenin-Macé et al., 2013.

claim: Targeting of Golgi-localised proteins by mycolactone leads to significantly decreased abundance of multiple enzymes involved in both higher order N- and O-linked glycosylation.
source: Detailed analysis of our dataset revealed that targeting of Golgi-localised proteins by mycolactone leads to significantly decreased abundance of multiple enzymes involved in both higher order N- and O-linked glycosylation (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on proteomic data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The effects of mycolactone on protein glycosylation may be even more far-reaching than expected, as even molecules resistant to the Sec61 blockade at the protein level may be functionally affected due to the loss of glycosylation.
source: It also suggests that the effects of mycolactone may be even more far-reaching than expected, as even molecules resistant to the Sec61 blockade at the protein level may be functionally affected due to the loss of glycosylation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proteomic data showing loss of glycosylation enzymes.

claim: Loss of one of the GAG linker-building enzymes common to CS, DS, and HS could be sufficient to explain the mycolactone-induced phenotype.
source: Since GAG biosynthesis is a sequential process, and the endothelial glycocalyx is essential to maintain monolayer permeability (Harding et al., 2019), we reasoned that loss of one of the GAG linker-building enzymes common to CS, DS, and HS could be sufficient to explain the mycolactone-induced phenotype.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proteomic data and cited literature.

claim: Children born with 'linkeropathies', who have a reduced ability to synthesise GAG linker regions, display phenotypes such as skin fragility and delayed wound healing that are similar to antibiotic-treated M. ulcerans infections.
source: In the context of BU, it is interesting to note that children born with 'linkeropathies', who have a reduced ability to synthesise GAG linker regions (Colman et al., 2019; Mihalic Mosher et al., 2019), display phenotypes such as skin fragility and delayed wound healing (Malfait et al., 2013) that are similar to antibiotic-treated M. ulcerans infections.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Colman et al., 2019, Mihalic Mosher et al., 2019, and Malfait et al., 2013.

claim: Loss of the glycocalyx could exacerbate the inhibition of leukocyte homing caused by mycolactone.
source: As well as increasing permeability, the loss of the glycocalyx could exacerbate the inhibition of leukocyte homing caused by mycolactone (Guenin-Macé et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference based on the current findings and cited literature.

claim: Other viral and bacterial pathogens promote colonisation by degrading the endothelial glycocalyx.
source: Notably other viral and bacterial pathogens promote colonisation by degrading the endothelial glycocalyx (Puerta-Guardo et al., 2016; Chiu et al., 2021; Tang et al., 2021); however, here the mechanism is via inducing the production of heparanase and other proteinases.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Puerta-Guardo et al., 2016, Chiu et al., 2021, and Tang et al., 2021.

claim: Adequate adhesion to the basement membrane is critical for endothelial cell proliferation, migration, morphogenesis and survival.
source: Adequate adhesion to the BM is critical for endothelial cell proliferation, migration, morphogenesis and survival (Davis and Senger, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Davis and Senger, 2005.

claim: Loss of perlecan and laminin α4, or reduced binding to fibronectin, disturbs the structural integrity and maturation of microvessels.
source: Furthermore, loss of perlecan and laminin α4, or reduced binding to fibronectin, disturbs the structural integrity and maturation of microvessels (Thyboll et al., 2002; Gustafsson et al., 2013; Nicosia et al., 1993), Finally, laminin α5 not only guides tissue patterning (Spenlé et al., 2013) and development (Miner et al., 1998) but also maintains vascular homeostasis by stabilising endothelial cell tight junctions (Song et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Thyboll et al., 2002, Gustafsson et al., 2013, and Nicosia et al., 1993.

claim: Laminin α5 guides tissue patterning and development.
source: Furthermore, loss of perlecan and laminin α4, or reduced binding to fibronectin, disturbs the structural integrity and maturation of microvessels (Thyboll et al., 2002; Gustafsson et al., 2013; Nicosia et al., 1993), Finally, laminin α5 not only guides tissue patterning (Spenlé et al., 2013) and development (Miner et al., 1998) but also maintains vascular homeostasis by stabilising endothelial cell tight junctions (Song et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Spenlé et al., 2013 and Miner et al., 1998.

claim: Laminin α5 maintains vascular homeostasis by stabilising endothelial cell tight junctions.
source: Furthermore, loss of perlecan and laminin α4, or reduced binding to fibronectin, disturbs the structural integrity and maturation of microvessels (Thyboll et al., 2002; Gustafsson et al., 2013; Nicosia et al., 1993), Finally, laminin α5 not only guides tissue patterning (Spenlé et al., 2013) and development (Miner et al., 1998) but also maintains vascular homeostasis by stabilising endothelial cell tight junctions (Song et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Song et al., 2017.

claim: The effects of mycolactone on the basement membrane may be exacerbated by IL-1β in vivo.
source: It is possible that these effects are exacerbated by IL-1β in vivo; this Sec61-independent pro-inflammatory cytokine has been shown to be induced in macrophages by mycolactone and M. ulcerans (Foulon et al., 2020; Hall et al., 2021) and is known to have profound effects on endothelial cell function, including the downregulation of anticoagulant and junctional proteins, induction of vascular permeability and upregulation of BM degrading proteinases (Cottam et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on cited literature.

claim: There is considerable overlap in the endothelial cell responses to IL-1β and mycolactone.
source: There is considerable overlap in the endothelial cell responses to IL-1β and mycolactone, although the former's effects are mediated predominantly at the transcriptional level.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of IL-1β and mycolactone mechanisms.

claim: An additive effect of mycolactone and IL-1β has been shown for some endothelial cell phenotypes in vitro.
source: An additive effect of mycolactone has been shown for some of these phenotypes in vitro (Ogbechi et al., 2015; Hsieh et al., 2022), although the in vivo situation is likely more complex (Hall et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ogbechi et al., 2015, Hsieh et al., 2022, and Hall et al., 2021.

claim: Loss/disruption of the endothelial glycocalyx and basement membrane is a critical molecular process in the pathogenesis of Buruli ulcer.
source: In summary, this study identifies loss/disruption of the endothelial glycocalyx and BM as a critical molecular process in the pathogenesis of Buruli ulcer.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the authors' interpretation of their findings.

claim: The effects of mycolactone on endothelial glycocalyx and basement membrane were the same with mycolactone extracted from M. ulcerans bacteria and chemically synthesised material.
source: These effects were the same with mycolactone extracted from M. ulcerans bacteria and chemically synthesised material, supporting the physiological relevance of our findings.
evidence: This is based on experimental data comparing synthetic and biological mycolactone.

claim: The changes in endothelial glycocalyx and basement membrane induced by mycolactone occur prior to mycolactone-driven apoptosis.
source: Since these changes occur prior to mycolactone-driven apoptosis (Ogbechi et al., 2018; Bieri et al., 2017; Ogbechi et al., 2015), they provide further support for our working model whereby mycolactone builds a hyper-coagulative environment alongside disruption of the endothelial monolayer and BM integrity.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ogbechi et al., 2018, Bieri et al., 2017, and Ogbechi et al., 2015.

claim: Mycolactone builds a hyper-coagulative environment alongside disruption of the endothelial monolayer and basement membrane integrity, leading to leakage of high molecular weight plasma proteins into the connective tissue where they activate the coagulation cascade leading to fibrin deposition and tissue ischemia.
source: We propose that this leads to leakage of high molecular weight plasma proteins into the connective tissue where they activate the coagulation cascade leading to fibrin deposition and tissue ischemia.
evidence: This is the authors' proposed model based on their findings.

claim: The detection of extravascular fibrinogen at early stages of M. ulcerans infection prior to widespread tissue damage and necrosis provides further evidence that endothelial dysfunction could be a driver of disease progression.
source: The detection of extravascular fibrinogen at early stages of infection prior to widespread tissue damage and necrosis provides further evidence that endothelial dysfunction could be a driver of disease progression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the in vivo data showing early fibrinogen deposition.

claim: Rethinking of Buruli ulcer as a vascular disease may ultimately lead to improved therapies that support better wound healing, alongside antibiotic treatment.
source: Rethinking of BU as a vascular disease may ultimately lead to improved therapies that support better wound healing, alongside antibiotic treatment.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future therapeutic approaches.

claim: Tissue repair requires a controlled progression through a series of different stages.
source: However, it should be remembered that tissue repair requires a controlled progression through a series of different stages Barker and Engler, 2017; following injury, under normal circumstances, platelet accumulation in a fibrin and fibronectin rich matrix is followed by an inflammation phase (Clark et al., 1982).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Barker and Engler, 2017 and Clark et al., 1982.

claim: Ameliorating the coagulative features with anticoagulants alongside the standard antimycobacterial drugs may be of most value in the initial stages of Buruli ulcer treatment.
source: Therefore, ameliorating the coagulative features with anticoagulants alongside the standard antimycobacterial drugs may be of most value in the initial stages of treatment, while bioactive dressings containing laminin-derived peptides might be more useful to promote healing at later stages.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic approaches.

claim: Bioactive dressings containing laminin-derived peptides might be useful to promote healing at later stages of Buruli ulcer treatment.
source: Therefore, ameliorating the coagulative features with anticoagulants alongside the standard antimycobacterial drugs may be of most value in the initial stages of treatment, while bioactive dressings containing laminin-derived peptides might be more useful to promote healing at later stages.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic approaches.

claim: Laminin-derived bioactive peptides have been proposed as a treatment for defective tissue repair.
source: In this context, laminin-derived bioactive peptides have recently been proposed as a treatment for defective tissue repair (Iorio et al., 2015) and indeed, accelerate re-epithelialisation in wounds of diabetic animals (Zhu et al., 2018; Ishihara et al., 2018), suggesting this novel approach may be an effective complement to current therapies and could alleviate the long wound healing times experienced by BU patients.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Iorio et al., 2015, Zhu et al., 2018, and Ishihara et al., 2018.

claim: Laminin-derived bioactive peptides accelerate re-epithelialisation in wounds of diabetic animals.
source: In this context, laminin-derived bioactive peptides have recently been proposed as a treatment for defective tissue repair (Iorio et al., 2015) and indeed, accelerate re-epithelialisation in wounds of diabetic animals (Zhu et al., 2018; Ishihara et al., 2018), suggesting this novel approach may be an effective complement to current therapies and could alleviate the long wound healing times experienced by BU patients.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Zhu et al., 2018 and Ishihara et al., 2018.

claim: Laminin-derived peptides may be an effective complement to current Buruli ulcer therapies and could alleviate the long wound healing times experienced by patients.
source: In this context, laminin-derived bioactive peptides have recently been proposed as a treatment for defective tissue repair (Iorio et al., 2015) and indeed, accelerate re-epithelialisation in wounds of diabetic animals (Zhu et al., 2018; Ishihara et al., 2018), suggesting this novel approach may be an effective complement to current therapies and could alleviate the long wound healing times experienced by BU patients.
